senses: To give something its own individuality; to characterize or differentiate.
To modify something to suit an individual; to personalize.
A person who uses hypnotism to induce hypnosis in someone, either for entertainment or therapy.
The coastal land bordering a sea or ocean.
ety: From Middle English see-cost, see-coste, see coost, equivalent to sea + coast. Compare West Frisian seekoast (“seacoast”), Dutch zeekust (“seacoast”), German Seeküste (“seacoast”).
examples: Neither chick nor child was left living the length of the seacoast.

senses: An annoying child, a brat.
examples: Get off my lawn, you little perisher!

senses: A dining room, especially one on an upper floor (traditionally the room in which the Last Supper took place).
A small circle or gathering of specialists (writers etc).
ety: From Middle English cenacle, from Old French cenacle (modern French cénacle), from Latin cēnāculum (“dining room”).
examples: I remember an anecdote of a well-known French theorist, who was debating a point eagerly in his cenacle. It was objected against him that he had never experienced love.

senses: Conversion to a decimal system.

Specifically, conversion of the currencies of the United Kingdom and Ireland in 1971 from pounds, shillings and pence to a decimal system in which one pound was worth 100 new pence (later renamed simply pence).
Disposed to shirk; tending to avoid work, obligations, etc.
Healthcare facilitated by telecommunication technology, typically allowing a doctor or other healthcare professional to interact with a patient visually and audibly.
examples: For millions of people like Poteat, pandemic-era telehealth flexibilities have made health care much more accessible.
In 2023, WeightWatchers bought the telehealth start-up, Sequence, for $106mn.

senses: A thin frame in a printing press that holds the sheet of paper in position and acts as a mask.
examples: As the pressman returns the inkballs to the inkstone, the journeyman closes the frisket and tympan.

senses: Following or relating to a formula; formulaic.
Having the characteristics of a tiger.
ety: From Middle English *tigrish, *tygrisch, from Old English tigrisċ (“of a tiger; tigerish”), equivalent to tiger + -ish.

senses: A Greek storeroom or warehouse.
ety: Borrowed from Ancient Greek ᾰ̓ποθήκη (ăpothḗkē). Doublet of bodega and boutique.
examples: The absence of earrings from the pre-Persian apothekes and the fact that only one was found on the South Hill indicate that earrings were infrequently used in archaic times at Olynthus.
Three hitherto unknown figures and other fragments from the Nike Balustrade found in the apothekes of the Museum are being published by I. Meliades.
During studies in apothekes and libraries, I have come to meet many new friends and colleagues, a part of the work that is just as important as the results from a personal point of view.

senses: Shaped like or resembling drops.
ety: Partly borrowed from Latin guttātus, partly from gutta + -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

senses: Being a heterotroph.
Full of feelings of regret, indulging in regrets.
Sorrowful about what has been lost or done.
examples: I continued also the wish to be with you, and experienced a strange, regretful consciousness of some barrier dividing us.
There was a feeling of utter desolation in my heart, filling it with a despairing and regretful sense, that I had not gone down with Robert to the bottom of the sea.
Huck scanned his own clothing forlornly. "I reckon I ain't dressed fitten for a pirate," said he, with a regretful pathos in his voice; "but I ain't got none but these."

senses: Rogue, adventurer.
Unusual or pathological sensitivity of the skin or of a particular sense.
That echoes; having an echoing quality.
Spanish mile, a traditional Spanish unit of distance equivalent to about 1.4 km.
ety: From Spanish milla (“Spanish mile”), from Latin mīlia (“Roman mile”), plural of mīlle (“1000”) in reference to its composition of 1000 Roman paces. Doublet of mile and milha.

senses: A form of Japanese contemporary dance.
ety: From Japanese 舞踏 (butō). The trailing “h” is to indicate the pronunciation; compare bokeh.

senses: A kind of light gig (open, two-wheeled carriage for one horse)
A person who operates a radio transceiver, especially when a title or position in a crew.
Having a thread across the field of view.
A system of government in which the people have virtually no authority and the state wields absolute control, for example, a dictatorship.
ety: 1938, from totalitarian + -ism, modeled after Italian totalitarismo (1923, by Giovanni Amendola) and German terms such as Totalstaat (1927, The Concept of the Political, by Carl Schmitt).
examples: Now, with her new book Beyond the Wall, Hoyer is seeking to retrieve the GDR from being written off as a chilling “footnote in German history”, a miserably grey country synonymous with unflinching totalitarianism.

senses: To finish or be finished; used to express that something is over or cannot be undone.
The act of immortalizing, or state of being immortalized
The act or process of arranging in alphabetical order.
A measure of the extent to which something is hydrophilic.
A soft Italian unsalted whey cheese resembling cottage cheese.
ety: Borrowed from Italian ricotta (literally “cooked again”), from Latin recocta.

senses: A movement of people from cities to rural coastal areas.
An act of relocating from an urban to a rural coastal community.
ety: From sea + change; sense 1 (“movement of people from cities to rural coastal areas; act of relocating from an urban to a rural coastal community”) was possibly coined by the Australian author and demographer Bernard Salt in his book The Big Shift (2001), based on the title of the Australian television series SeaChange (1998–2000 and 2019) about a lawyer who moved with her daughters from the city to a coastal town.

senses: The name of an ethnic group, nation, nationality, tribe, tribal alliance, clan, or other ethnic community.
The knocking down of all nine pins in one go.
Not myelinated.
To change the culture of (a person) by the influence of another culture, especially a more dominant culture.
To be changed by acculturation.
ety: * Back-formation from acculturation; first attested in 1923

senses: One of the leading missionaries of the Hashimiyya movement who prepared the Abbasid Revolution in Khurasan.
The head representative of the ashraf, the descendants of Muhammad; an honorary position in the Ottoman Empire.
Tending or seeming to drift.
Based upon, or resembling, the sound of a synthesizer.
its flesh as a seafood.
ety: From Lushootseed gʷidəq, variously understood as reference to its deep digging or resemblance to male genitalia. The unusual spelling of the first syllable is thought to represent editorial hypercorrection of forms with goe- &c. (probably under influence from the common prefix geo-), despite the earlier attestation of forms with geo-. The spelling pronunciation /ˈdʒiːəʊdʌk/ once listed in dictionaries is now considered nonstandard. The common spelling of the second syllable is under influence from duck, originally with reference to the mollusc's resemblance to the body and neck of a dead duck.

senses: The plant Camelina sativa, sometimes cultivated for oilseed.
examples: Another possibility is camelina, which produces a tiny, mustardlike seed from which oil can be extracted, It does not require extensive fertilization.

senses: A viewpoint or theory that places human beings at the center of everything, giving preference to human beings above all other considerations.
